The government has approved the agreement and submitted it to the Constitutional Court. The court must now determine whether it complies with Armenia’s constitution.

“If the Constitutional Court finds that the obligations set out in this international agreement are compatible with Armenia’s constitution, we will submit it to the National Assembly in accordance with the established procedure and bring it before parliament for discussion,” Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said, outlining the next steps. Parliament must ratify the agreement before it can take effect.

Mirzoyan said Armenia must also finalise two more documents before it can complete the TRIPP project. They include a shareholders’ agreement and the charter of the TRIPP Development Company.

The foreign minister also commented on reports about the TRIPP+ fund. Britain’s The Guardian reported on the fund a day earlier, prompting questions in Armenia about the new structure. Mirzoyan said it was an American investment fund and would have only “an indirect connection” with the company that Armenia plans to establish.

Armenia and the United States initialled the framework agreement on strategic cooperation under the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity project on 26 May 2026. Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio took part in the initialling ceremony in Yerevan. They signed the agreement shortly afterwards through a remote procedure. Rubio signed it in Washington on 1 June, while Mirzoyan signed it in Yerevan on 4 June. “To dispel any possible questions, I would like to note that international practice and Armenian legislation both provide for the signing of such non-simultaneous, remote agreements, and this is a widely accepted practice,” Ararat Mirzoyan said during today’s government meeting. On 8 August 2025, the leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the United States signed a joint declaration at a summit in Washington, marking the launch of the regional connectivity project. The declaration mentioned the Trump Route project for the first time. Before that, Armenia and Azerbaijan had failed to reach agreement on the issue. Azerbaijan had demanded a route it called the “Zangezur Corridor”. Armenia said it was ready to reopen all transport links. At the same time, it firmly rejected the term “corridor”, arguing that it implied the loss of sovereign rights over its territory. The parties reached a compromise only in Washington. They agreed that Armenia would retain sovereign control over the route, while the United States would join the project as a business partner.

“Armenia and the US will help strengthen peace in the South Caucasus”

According to Armenia’s foreign minister, the TRIPP project will help bring peace, stability and prosperity to the South Caucasus. He said it would achieve this by promoting:

transport connectivity;

infrastructure development; and

regional and global trade.

Under the framework agreement, Armenia and the United States will establish the TRIPP Development Company. The company will have the authority to create special purpose entities and bring in additional partners to implement individual projects in Armenia.

“The entire process, from the establishment of the development company to its future operations, will fully respect Armenia’s sovereignty, jurisdiction and territorial integrity,” Ararat Mirzoyan said.

He recalled that the development company would receive land use and development rights for the relevant areas. The parties have set the initial term at 49 years. The United States will hold a 74% stake in the company, while Armenia will own the remaining 26%. If the partnership continues for another 50 years, Armenia’s share will automatically increase to 49% after the first 49-year term.

“If the term is extended, Armenia will not need to take any additional steps to obtain its 49% stake,” the minister said.

Armenia will retain control over border, customs and migration procedures

The foreign minister again stressed that, in line with Armenia’s domestic legislation and international agreements, the Armenian authorities will continue to oversee:

security and the protection of rights;

border control and border security;

customs and migration procedures;

the collection of taxes and customs duties for the state budget;

state information systems; and

public administrative functions.

He said these guarantees should address public concerns about Armenia retaining its sovereign rights over the territory.

What is the link between the TRIPP Development Company and TRIPP+?

Britain’s The Guardian reported that the US State Department had appointed Konstantin Sokolov to lead the TRIPP+ trade fund. Sokolov is a US investor who was born in the Soviet Union and now lives in Chicago.

Armenian media quickly picked up the report. However, questions remained about the nature of the fund and its relationship with the company that Armenia plans to establish to implement the Trump Route project.

Journalists raised the issue during the government meeting. Ararat Mirzoyan replied that the agreement between Yerevan and Washington provides for the creation of the TRIPP Development Company.

“Its founders will be the Armenian government and the TRIPP Development Company-USA, which will be established in the United States,” Mirzoyan said.

As for TRIPP+, he said it is an American company established under the TRIPP Development Company-USA. Its role will be to attract investment for the project.

“From a legal perspective, TRIPP+ has only an indirect relationship with the TRIPP Development Company that will be established in Armenia,” the minister said..

Armenia begins ratifying the TRIPP agreement

World.title: Pauline Hanson 'not backing away' from controversial far-right interview
World.content:
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says she does not regret being interviewed by far-right UK figure Tommy Robinson.

During a podcast interview last week with Robinson, Senator Hanson blamed the end of the White Australia policy for migration issues in Australia.

She also suggested, without providing evidence, that Muslim Australians were prominent in rorting the National Disability Insurance Scheme.

The One Nation leader's comments have drawn sharp criticism from figures across Labor, the Coalition and the Greens.

During a segment on Seven's Spotlight program, Senator Hanson was filmed recording the podcast and walking with Tommy Robinson through Luton, north-west of London, which has a significant Muslim population.

Tommy Robinson has an extensive criminal record and is shunned by major British parties (Reuters: Chris J Ratcliffe)

Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, is a far-right anti-immigration figure in the UK with an extensive criminal record, who has served prison sentences for fraud and assault.

Nigel Farage, the leader of the far-right party Reform UK, has frequently sought to distance himself from Robinson and quit his former UK Independence Party when Robinson joined.

Senator Hanson was asked during the program if appearing alongside Tommy Robinson risked harming her reputation.

Taylor rules out One Nation coalition Coalition leader Angus Taylor has renewed his criticism of Pauline Hanson's party and categorically ruled out any alliance with it.

"Why wouldn't I talk to the man? Am I going to be judged by all those people — I shouldn't be associating, talking to this man. That's the problem with our society," she told Channel 7.

"I'm not like the other politicians, I will say and do what I want to.

"I will talk to people, to spend time and learn from them about what is happening."

Pushed on whether she was "aligning" herself with Robinson, Senator Hanson defended the decision.

"I'm sorry, I'm not going to back away from this whatsoever," she said.

" I met Tommy and I listened to what he is trying to tell me about what has happened to Britain. "

Hanson says she 'doesn't believe' in White Australia policy

Senator Hanson has spent weeks travelling through the UK and Europe, addressing conservative conferences and attending a fashion show in Italy alongside billionaire Gina Rinehart.

She delivered a speech to a half-empty room at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in London, railing against Australia's immigration and environmental policies and telling the crowd the country had "gone woke".

Pauline Hanson gave a speech at a conservative political conference in front of a sparse crowd in London. (ABC News: Riley Stuart)

She declined to answer a question from the ABC about who funded her travels to Italy, and avoided speaking to reporters while at the conference.

But in a clip posted to social media, she rejected suggestions she said had been made that she wanted to "introduce the White Australia policy".

"Never ever have I advocated that, and I don't believe in it as well," she said.

But she said it is true that she "doesn't want people from certain countries that wear the burqa".

During the Spotlight interview, Senator Hanson was asked her view on the "concept of mass deportation".

"Oh I love it," she told the network.

She said she has the full support of her colleagues in her support for the idea, but clarified she was targeting "the ones who are here illegally in the country".

One Nation has a listed immigration policy of deporting 75,000 "illegal migrants" including "visa overstayers, illegal workers, and unlawful non-residents".

World.title: Israel says Iran has launched missiles towards Jordan
World.content:
The United States has warned its citizens to stay away from air and sea ports in the southern Jordanian city of Aqaba, hours before Israeli authorities announced that Iranian missiles had been launched towards the city.

The notice was issued by the US Embassy in the Jordanian capital Amman on Sunday afternoon local time, after what it said was a "specific and credible threat," and followed days of sustained attacks by Iran on the Middle Eastern kingdom.

However, Jordan's state news agency, citing a government spokesperson, had said neither the Aqaba airport or port had been evacuated and there were no potential threats detected in recent hours, fuelling confusion about what was actually happening.

Around two hours after the US warning, the Israeli military confirmed it had detected incoming Iranian missiles.

Aqaba's airport is just a few kilometres from the Jordan-Israel border, and the southern Israeli city of Eilat.

US strikes 'punish' Iran for troop deaths The US and Iran have intensified attacks since an interim ceasefire deal signed a month ago fell apart, raising the possibility of a return to all-out war.

Later on Sunday, Jordan announced via its state news agency that it had shot down three missiles, while a fourth fell in a remote area.

There were no injuries or "material damage", it added.

Jordan is one of the US's closest allies in the region, and American military personnel operate out of a number of bases across the country.

Two American soldiers were killed in one such Iranian attack over the weekend, while a third is missing.

Video circulating on social media, which has not been verified by the ABC, reportedly showed a barrage of attacks on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, roughly 100 kilometres east of Amman.

Iran has said that US bases and soldiers operating across the Persian Gulf and beyond are fair targets, after an eighth consecutive day of American attacks hit the Islamic Republic.

US Central Command said Iranian surveillance systems and missile and drone storage sites were hit in the latest round of attacks.

People inspect a bridge damaged in southern Iran on Saturday. (AP: Amirhosein Khorgooi)

Iranian state media, citing the country's atomic energy agency, said the US had hit a site of a nuclear power plant, still being built, in the Darkhovin region.

It was not clear whether that was a strike during the latest wave of attacks, or happened earlier in the week.

Warning sirens rang out across Kuwait and Bahrain for hours after, with Iran following its pattern of hitting the beleaguered Gulf states in response.

Mojtaba Khamenei's whereabouts remain a mystery

The ongoing Iranian attacks, particularly those targeted at Jordan, have cast doubt on the repeated insistence by the US and Israel that many of the regime's launchers and stockpiles had been destroyed earlier in the war.

It was just over a month ago that the US president signed a deal to immediately end fighting, and begin negotiations with Iran on a lasting peace.

A woman holds a portraits of Iran's supreme leaders, past and present. (Reuters: Teba Sadiq)

Since then the White House has accused Iran of welching on the deal, and Iran has argued it would not negotiate with the US while under sustained threats of attack.

Adding to the complexity of the situation is the continued absence of Iran's new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei.

The eight words important to Iran Iran's lead negotiator makes it very clear where the regime stands on the Strait of Hormuz.

He has not been seen in public since succeeding his father Ali Khamenei, not appearing appearing at his weeklong funeral alongside his brothers.

For months, speculation has swirled that he was severely injured in the strike which killed his father on the very first day of the war, and has been left with significant disfigurement.

Saudi news outlet Al Hadath, citing an Israeli security source, has reported he is not even believed to be in Iran, and the statements being attributed to him and read out on state television are actually written by advisors and members of the powerful Revolutionary Guard.

Over the weekend another of those missives was broadcast to the country, using familiar rhetoric to criticise the US.

"The repeated breaches of covenant by the Great Satan regarding the memorandum of understanding signed between the presidents of Iran and the United States once again proved to everyone this truth: that the signature of the President of the United States is utterly worthless and invalid," Ayatollah Khamenei's statement said.

"Bullying, hegemonic ambition, and savagery are inseparable components of the American creed and way of conduct.

"Now that the American enemy seeks to foment war and to bear even heavier costs and greater disgrace, it should know that the beloved nation of Iran and the Resistance Front have unforgettable lessons in store for it."

The struggle over Strait of Hormuz

The return to fighting had been fuelled by the dispute over the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow shipping channel Iran shut down at the height of the war.

The Revolutionary Guard said four ships tried to get through the waterway using an "unsafe route" on Sunday, switching off their electronic tracking signals in the process.

"Two of them were involved in accidents and stopped where they were, while the other two abandoned their course," a statement read out on Iranian state media said.

Trump ditches Hormuz fee plan Donald Trump reneges on his pledge to charge a 20 per cent fee on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after saying he would introduce it.

Last week, Mr Trump announced plans for the US to take control of the Strait of Hormuz and charge Gulf states a fee for transit.

He dropped the second part of the proposal hours before it was due to come into force, after lobbying from the countries which would have footed the bill.

But the US has reimposed a blockade on all Iranian ports and ships in the region, and Iran has threatened to use its proxies in Yemen, the Houthis, to shut down another shipping lane — the Bab El Mandeb Strait, which is the gateway to the Red Sea.

While the continuous strikes between the US and Iran have signalled the ceasefire between the two countries is over, fighting has not returned to the intensity of March and April.

Israel, one of the instigators in the conflict, has also not re-entered the fray.

Israeli media is reporting more US aircraft, both fighter jets and refuelling planes, have been sent to the region ahead of a potential escalation.

While Israel is broadly supportive of the war, the presence of US Air Force planes at the country's main airport has led to significant disruptions.

Some large aircraft are taking up space at Ben Gurion Airport, limiting the number of commercial flights that can operate from Tel Aviv during the busy summer tourist season.

World.title: Piastri overcomes early knock as teen sensation triumphs in Belgian GP
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli has extended his lead at the top of the F1 championship standings with victory in the Belgian Grand Prix, with George Russell crashing out in the first lap and Oscar Piastri overcoming an early knock to finish fifth.

Piastri suffered minor damage to his car in the incident which saw him collide with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc, who was cleared of wrongdoing by race officials and went on to claim second place.

And Piastri, who won this race last year, recovered well to ensure he finished in the scoring places behind Antonelli, with Max Verstappen third behind Leclerc.

Lewis Hamilton was placed fourth, but his Ferrari team are under investigation for an unsafe release, so there could yet be a change of order.

The incident followed another early controversy when Russell was forced to retire on the first lap after a prang with fellow Briton Hamilton to deal a huge blow to the Mercedes man's title hopes.

Russell, who had started third on the grid was attempting to overtake Hamilton when his rear wheel was tagged by the Ferrari driver, sending him spinning into the gravel and forcing the arrival of the safety car.

Russell drops to third in the drivers' championship and was fuming with the outcome having lost further ground on title leader Antonelli, and was once again left baffled by a mystery engine issue causing a speed deficit.

"I just got totally swallowed up down the straight, I lost three positions down the straight, down into turn five, then the incident was a racing incident," Russell told the host broadcaster.

"Maybe I could have gone a bit wider, maybe he could've braked a bit more.

"The incident shouldn't have happened if I had the speed down the straight.

"Very, very disappointing … felt like I was in a position to fight for the lead after turn one and suddenly no power and it's all gone."

Russell was bitterly disappointed with his early exit from the race. (Getty Images: Clive Mason)

The victory was the sixth of the season for teenage driver Antonelli and the first since last month's Monaco Grand Prix, which leaves him 45 points clear of Russell in the championship.

"Let's go!" he screamed to the Mercedes team over the radio.

"Thank you so much, guys, thank you."

Piastri's McLaren team-mate, Lando Norris, started 13th due to a grid penalty but he still finished seventh after a pit-stop delay.

Frenchman Isack Hadjar finished sixth behind Piastri for Red Bull, despite starting at the back of the field because of a penalty.

AAP/ABC

Relive all the action in our live blog below.

World.title: Rules to tighten on AI use in decision-making by government departments
World.content:
Australia will tighten oversight of artificial intelligence in automated government decision-making and strengthen privacy safeguards as part of a broader push to allay concerns about the technology's risks to community safety.

A new list of AI consumer priorities published by the government on Sunday includes a promise to "better regulate" the use of AI in federal agencies like Centrelink and Services Australia, and revisit personal data protection laws.

Pressure has been building on the government to commit to human intervention in the administration of government schemes, particularly in social services, balanced with a desire to use emerging technology to boost productivity.

AI standards to set data centre rules The prime minister unveils Labor's plan for new AI national standards, warning Australia has a narrow window to set AI's "social licence".

In May, Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth said humans would remain involved in the Jobseeker payment process as she announced an overhaul of the unemployment system.

Last year, the Commonwealth Ombudsman found almost a thousand jobseekers had their income support payments unlawfully terminated via automatic cancellations.

The government has also faced scrutiny over automated elements of the aged care home support program, as well as a planning tool in the National Disability Insurance Scheme that generates budgets for participants.

Earlier this year the ombudsman opened an investigation into the algorithm-based aged care assessment tool.

Echo of privacy legislation in consumer protection priority

The government has also committed to reconsider protections for consumers and singled out retail surveillance pricing, the practice of farming data to set different prices for individual consumers based on behaviour, as a priority issue.

In its first term, the government legislated a tranche of strengthened privacy protections for consumers but could not find support for a crackdown on advertising.

Copyright law battleground in Australia's AI boom Tens of billions of dollars in investment, and Australia's ambition to become a global AI power, could hinge on a law written in 1968 for an era of black-and-white television, film and radio.

Under the reforms proposed in 2024, Australians would have had the right to opt out of targeted advertising, including restrictions on the use of sensitive information.

The 'Consumer Protections' priority included in the AI list includes a promise to "examine options" in consumer law, led by Assistant Minister for Competition Andrew Leigh.

AI to dominate Labor conference

AI is expected to dominate debate at the National Labor Conference in Adelaide later this week, with a particular focus on workers' rights.

Delegates, parliamentarians and union leaders have until Wednesday to seek amendments to Labor's AI policy platform before a vote.

A draft of the policy platform indicates there will be a focus on the impact of AI across the economy, including jobs, and a commitment to hold AI companies accountable to Australian "values and laws."

Labor conference to test PM's AI pitch Labor insiders expect ongoing debate about artificial intelligence when party faithful gather to hash out a policy platform to guide the next three years.

It said there must be "transparency, accountability and fairness" for potential harms the models produce.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has previously said workers should recognise that "artificial intelligence is happening."

"Change is happening, and they have an interest in shaping that change because if not, then they don't get a say," he said.

The prime minister has also vowed not to let AI companies train their models using Australian books, music, art or music without compensation.

World.title: Asylum seekers sent to Nauru by Australia say they are going hungry
World.content:
Asylum seekers sent to Nauru by the Australian government say they are going hungry, despite the Commonwealth spending nearly $900 million to fund offshore detention in the last financial year.

The Asylum Seeker Resource Centre (ASRC) surveyed 78 asylum seekers on Nauru, with almost every one of them claiming they could not buy enough food with their fortnightly allowance of $260 and were regularly skipping meals.

More than three quarters of the asylum seekers surveyed said they rarely had access to free, clean drinking water.

While the Nauruan government ultimately determines the rate of payment based on the average local wage, Australia funds the program through its memorandum of understanding with Nauru.

"The cost of living is really high [on Nauru]," George*, an asylum seeker who has been on Nauru for nearly two years waiting for his refugee status to be resolved, told the ABC.

"Everybody is facing difficulties, and we have a food shortage. Fruit and vegetables and fresh meat are hard to find, and the price can be ridiculous.

"I eat discarded food from the bin of local restaurants, even though it makes me sick.

"Quite a few people are doing the same thing."

Most of the asylum seekers on Nauru are from Asian countries. (AAP: Department of Immigration)

George, whose name has been changed, is one of more than 160 people who have been sent to Nauru by the government since 2023, when Australia's offshore processing regime restarted.

About 100 remain on the island, and hail mostly from China, Pakistan and Bangladesh. They do not have work rights in Nauru, and face their stipend being cancelled if caught working illegally.

Nearly all those who spoke to the ASRC reported eating less often than they needed or wanted to.

"I sometimes only have one meal a day," George said.

" I try to catch fish from the sea but have injured myself doing this. "

Nauru is in the Pacific Ocean, about 3,000 kilometres north-east of Australia. (AP: Jason Oxenham)

Nauru relies almost entirely on imported food, with most fresh produce sold for well above typical supermarket prices in Australia.

ABC has not independently verified the claims of asylum seekers going hungry.

Most journalists, including from the ABC, are restricted from entering the island nation.

Australia has 'legal responsibility', UN says

Until recently, asylum seekers on Nauru received about $230 per fortnight to cover all their basic needs. In December 2025, the stipend was increased to $260 per fortnight.

That equates to $18 a day.

Iranians waiting years for asylum seeker status in Australia Iranian refugees in Australia welcome Iran's footballers being granted asylum, but question why others remain stuck on a years-long waitlist for permanent residency.

While the Nauruan government ultimately determines the rate of payment based on the average local wage, Australia funds the program through its memorandum of understanding with Nauru.

In 2025, the government struck a new, non-public agreement with Nauru to facilitate the removal of individuals held in immigration detention in Australia, after the High Court's NZYQ ruling, which found indefinite detention was illegal.

In May, a United Nations report found countries could not avoid legal responsibility for asylum seekers who arrived on their shores by "contracting out their obligations to other States".

"Rather than seeking to outsource responsibilities through arrangements that create human rights risks … states should prioritise rights-based, fair and sustainable asylum and migration systems that fully respect human rights and related procedural safeguards," the report said.

Of the 100 or so asylum seekers currently on Nauru, none will be able to come to Australia even if determined to be genuine refugees.

Offshore processing 'failed'

In the 2001 Tampa crisis, a Norwegian freighter rescued more than 400 asylum seekers from a sinking Indonesian fishing boat. (AAP)

Since the 2001 Tampa crisis, Australia has instituted a policy of offshore detention, upheld by successive Coalition and Labor governments.

The policy rationale is to deter asylum seekers from coming to Australia illegally by boat, by denying them resettlement pathways in Australia, and access to the legal system.

ASRC deputy CEO Jana Favero described Australia's policy of offshore processing as a "failure".

"In the last year alone, the Albanese government spent almost a billion dollars [on offshore processing]. And for what? A harmful and cruel policy where people don't have enough food and are going hungry," she said.

" It's outrageous and shameful. "

The Home Affairs Department said the fortnightly payment was "designed to promote self-sufficiency" and was reviewed regularly "to ensure it remains fit for purpose".

"People transferred and accommodated under regional processing arrangements are treated with respect and dignity and in accordance with human rights standards," a spokesperson said.

The government said individuals on Nauru had access to health and welfare services, and did not pay for their accommodation.

World.title: Russia pounds Kyiv in major ballistic missile attack
World.content:
Russia has battered Ukraine's capital Kyiv with one of its biggest ballistic missile barrages of the war, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

At least one person has been killed and 16 others wounded.

A series of powerful explosions thundered across the darkened city in an attack that involved 41 missiles of various types and ravaged buildings across several districts, overnight into Sunday, local time.

Smoke rises over Kyiv. (AP: Efrem Lukatsky)

Russia also launched 125 attack drones across Ukraine, according to the Ukrainian air force.

Residential buildings, warehouses, a supermarket and a dormitory were among the structures damaged, said Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko, adding that three people were in a serious condition.

President Zelenskyy posted on X:

"Overnight, Russia carried out one of its largest ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv. The enemy launched more than 40 missiles of various types — most of them against the capital".

The attack began about 1:30am local time and continued for several hours, according to officials.

Kyiv's acting foreign minister Andrii Sybiha called for "appropriate and strong responses" in a post on X, describing the night's events as a "brutal terrorist attack on the Ukrainian capital".

At one location in western Kyiv, emergency workers picked through smouldering debris and doused bombed-out apartments.

Debris surrounds a missile crater in Kyiv. (AP: Efrem Lukatsky)

A resident who identified himself as Vlad said he had been inside his apartment when a blast tore off his balcony door, which smashed him in the head.

"My grandmother lives with me, and she can't walk. How could I run away and leave her behind?" he said.

Closer to the city centre, an underground pedestrian passage near a frequently targeted metro station had caved in, leaving a pile of rubble.

Critical shortage of air defences

Russian forces have stepped up ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv and other cities in recent weeks as Ukraine struggles with a critical shortage of US-designed air defences.

Kyiv's military said it had shot down 18 missiles in Sunday's attack, which was aimed primarily at the Ukrainian capital.

The attack began about 1:30am local time and continued for several hours. (AP: Efrem Lukatsky)

It added that 108 out of 125 drones had also been downed.

Mr Zelenskyy said last week that the US and Ukraine had reached a political agreement on licences to make the prized Patriot interceptors.

He added that he hoped production could begin by the end of the year.

But the mounting Russian attacks in the fifth year of Moscow's full-scale war are heaping pressure on Kyiv's foreign partners to accelerate supply of anti-ballistic defences.

"Protection against ballistic missiles is our constant and top priority right now," Mr Zelenskyy said on X on Sunday.

"Interceptors are needed every day."

Reuters/AP

World.title: Special guest dazzles aspiring astronauts at Space Day Out
World.content:
The Australian Space Agency kicked off Australian Space Week on Sunday with a new event aimed at inspiring young people to pursue a career in space exploration.

The inaugural Space Day Out was held at the Australian Space Discovery Centre in Adelaide's Lot Fourteen precinct and attracted around 2,000 people.

Many had a close encounter of the hero kind when they met Australian astronaut and special guest Katherine Bennell-Pegg.

Nine-year-old Chase Iannuzzi from Melbourne was gifted the day out for his birthday and said he was excited to travel to Adelaide because he wanted to see "an actual real" astronaut.

That dream came true when he met 2026 Australian of the Year Ms Bennell-Pegg on Sunday.

"It was just so exciting," Chase said. "I'm really, really, really into space. Like, super. I have space Lego, space pictures … I think it's awesome. I really want to be the first person to go to Mars and Pluto."

Chase wants to visit Mars and Pluto.

Young fan and aspiring astronaut Alice also had stars in her eyes when she met Australia's first female astronaut.

"When I grow up I want to be an astronaut," Alice said. "I have since I was three. My biggest dream is going to space and walking on the moon."

She said Ms Bennell-Pegg loved the pink-and-white astronaut costume she wore to the event.

"It was really fun," Alice said. "I asked if she was a lefty or a righty, and she's a righty [handed]."

Nurturing the next generation

Ms Bennell-Pegg emphasised the importance of inspiring young people in STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) fields.

"Right now in Australia, we're leaving too much talent on the launch pad," she said.

"We're seeing the lowest-ever enrolments in Year 12 physics across the country and the lowest-ever enrolments in intermediate maths and in higher maths, and this at a time where we have so many issues facing us as a nation and globally.

"What I've seen since I've come back from astronaut training and got out and about across Australia is how space is a magnet to keep young people engaged with science and maths.

" It gives them something to aim for and that drive to get through the hard parts to a compelling breadth of different careers in STEM. "

Ms Bennell-Pegg said her focus for now was on speaking to young people and exciting them about space.

"Also, remaining match-fit for space, should that opportunity ever arise."

She highlighted Australia's engagement with the European Space Agency and the potential benefits for the nation's scientists and engineers.

"I'm excited not just for me, but for what it could do for our scientists, our engineers, and our future workforce," she said.

"But right now, my focus is on the ground. Most of an astronaut's career is on the ground, training and preparing for space."

Aspiring astronaut Alice had stars in her eyes when she met Australia's first female astronaut. (ABC News: Luke Pike)

Economic impact of reaching for the stars

Chris Picton, SA minister for defence and space industries, said space was pivotal to the state's economy across several sectors.

"Whether that's defence industries, whether that's agriculture which relies on space, but of course telecommunications as well," Mr Picton said.

"Space is becoming more important, and we want to be at the forefront of that here in South Australia. Having the Space Agency [and] having some of these key companies here in our state really give us the leading edge."

The head of the Australian Space Agency, Enrico Palermo, said space was critical to the nation's economy, defence, and understanding of navigation and weather systems.

"Today is a chance for young and old to engage with space, understand that criticality but also be inspired at a time when we really need to boost the number of students entering higher degree mathematics and physics," Mr Palermo said.

"South Australia is one of the leading growth states in terms of our space economy in Australia.

"In recent years, we've seen more than $75 million underpinned by investments by the National Reconstruction Fund."

He said the state had deep roots in the space sector, including Australia's first flights to space from the Woomera test range.

He also pointed to the importance of Lot Fourteen-based businesses, including satellite telecommunications company Myriota, and Southern Launch, which operates the Koonibba Test Range.

"That initial crucible of space startups started here in South Australia," he said.

Enrico Palermo says space is critical to the nation's economy, defence, and understanding of navigation and weather systems. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Close encounters of the aspirational kind

Mc Bennell-Pegg said one of the most common misconceptions about space was that it was a "nice to have".

"Whereas it's actually a 'need to have,'" she said.

"Space underpins our modern economy, our daily life, the breadth of science, and also prepares for our future by exciting young people about their futures in STEM."

She knows the power of a meet-and-greet all too well. During childhood, meeting her idols made space feel within reach.

"Becoming an astronaut was a childhood dream," she said.

"I remember growing up and having the chance to meet Paul Scully-Power and Andy Thomas, two Australians that have been to space but representing other nations.

"It was really impactful for me to see that they're just real people that had worked hard towards a dream and managed to get there."

World.title: Brondello suspended by WNBA for inappropriate comment
World.content:
Australian coach Sandy Brondello has been suspended for one game by the WNBA for an inappropriate comment she used during a Toronto Tempo game against the Atlanta Dream.

Brondello, who coaches the Tempo as well the Opals, will miss Tuesday's AEST game against the Las Vegas Aces.

"The WNBA expects all coaches and team personnel to uphold the highest standards of professionalism and respect that are fundamental to our league," the league said in a statement announcing the suspension.

During the 111-92 loss to the Dream on Saturday AEST, the broadcast picked up Brondello addressing officials after Tempo player Nyara Sabally went down with an injury following contact with Angel Reese.

Sabally was called for the foul and Brondello could be heard saying Reese was a "protected species".

The "protected species" phrase is commonly used in Australian sports to express frustration for a lack of calls against a player.

In the US, however, the phrase can be considered derogatory towards black people.

Angel Reese took to social media in response to Sandy Brondello's comment. (Getty Images: Mark Blinch)

Brondello posted an apology on social media.

"Angel, I'm sorry," Brondello wrote on X.

"Last night, in the emotion of the moment after Nyara's injury, I used a phrase that I shouldn't have used, and I take full responsibility for that. My frustration was with the officiating, but my words unfairly put the focus on you."

How Brondello hopes to topple US No country has been able to topple the United States at either the FIBA World Cup or the Olympics since 2006. Here's what Sandy Brondello is doing to try to get Australia's Opals over the hump.

Reese took to social media after the game, posting: "ARE WE SURPRISED?!" and tagging Brondello's account, followed by a clown face emoji.

"I also understand that my words carried an impact beyond what I intended, particularly for black women in our league, and I'm deeply sorry for that," Brondello posted.

"I've spent my career competing with, coaching and learning from incredible black women."

Brondello added: "I regret that my words caused hurt to a community I respect so deeply.

"I have a lot of respect for you as both a player and a person, and I sincerely apologise to you, your teammates, and the Dream organisation for my comment."

AP

World.title: ‘A bloody good feeling’: Essendon bask in the glow of landing a win, climbing off the bottom
World.content:
AFL Briefing SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘A bloody good feeling’: Essendon bask in the glow of landing a win, climbing off the bottom Oliver Caffrey , Ed Jackson , Nick Smart and Scott Spits Updated July 20, 2026 — 12:26am ,first published 4:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

In today’s AFL Briefing, your daily wrap of footy news: Western Bulldogs heaped more pressure on Gold Coast with a nine-point win.

Hawthorn dined out on lowly Richmond at the MCG on Sunday.

Carlton forward Harry McKay suffered bone bruising and a minor tear in his meniscus against Collingwood. Dons delight: Bombers end losing streak Oliver Caffrey An elated Dean Solomon has described Essendon’s stunning three-point upset of inconsistent GWS as a “bloody good feeling”. Having won just one of their previous 30 games, the Bombers finally played with a sense of urgency to give Solomon his first win in his 10th match as a caretaker coach, which includes three at Gold Coast in 2017.



Leading at every break, Essendon gave up their advantage twice in a frantic final term but hit back through clutch goals to Sullivan Robey and Peter Wright. Sheer wonder: Jacob Farrow of the Bombers. Getty Images With a wildcard spot still up for grabs, the Giants desperately tried to reclaim the lead in the dying stages, but Essendon hung on for a famous win - 10.7 (67) to 8.16 (64) - amid scenes of delirium in front of a small, but vocal crowd at Marvel Stadium. It was Essendon’s first win since beating Melbourne in Gather Round in Adelaide on April 11, while they hadn’t won a game in Victoria since May 2025. The Bombers, who were ravaged by Brisbane last Sunday and had lost 12-straight matches, were given virtually no hope of matching it with the red-hot Giants.



“It’s a bloody good feeling,” Solomon said. Pumped: Dean Solomon with Zach Merrett. Getty Images “Our footy club’s been on its knees for a period of time, and the footy world’s jumped on that, and they enjoy us sitting at the bottom. “We’ve felt that, and we don’t like that, so to push back a little bit and get one win, albeit one win, I’m just really happy for these players.” The result continued GWS’s baffling trend of struggling against lower-ranked opposition whilst also dismantling last year’s grand finalists Brisbane and Geelong, and rampaging ladder-leaders Fremantle, amid their previous seven games.



As well as the Bombers, GWS have dropped matches to St Kilda (twice) and West Coast. “It was incredibly disappointing,” Giants coach Adam Kingsley said. “The messaging around our consistency, our ability to perform against every team in the competition, not just those who were above us.” In a further concern for the Giants, they lost captain Toby Greene to a serious-looking quad injury in the third quarter that will almost certainly mean he misses the Sydney derby against the Swans next Saturday. Further delighting the home crowd, former Essendon forward Jake Stringer endured a horror match in front of goal to finish with 0.7 on a wayward night for the Giants.



View post on X The only concern for Essendon was young star Nate Caddy, who was sent to hospital due to an elevated heart rate. Caddy, who recently re-signed until the end of 2031 in a massive boost for the battling Bombers, didn’t return to the ground after quarter-time. Solomon revealed Caddy had been able to leave hospital, but would undergo further tests during the week.



“To do it without him is sad in one instance, but it’s also a pretty super effort from this group,” Solomon said. The result could prove costly for GWS, who would have jumped into 10th and a wildcard spot, had they beaten the Bombers. It also lifted Essendon to 17th, sending Richmond to the bottom of the ladder. View post on X AAP



Bulldogs pile more misery on Suns in nine-point win Gold Coast coach Damien Hardwick believes his team is falling short in critical moments after a nine-point loss to the Western Bulldogs. The 11.11 (77) to 9.14 (68) defeat on Sunday at a blustery People First Stadium was the Suns’ eighth consecutive defeat, further eroding their slim hopes of sneaking into a top 10 position. For the Bulldogs, the victory cements them in seventh and gives them breathing space over the chasing pack in and around that crucial 10th position on the ladder.



Gold Coast’s loss came despite the Suns having 91 more disposals, nine more clearances and 11 more inside 50s than the visitors. Roaring with delight: Ed Richards of the Bulldogs. AFL Photos Hardwick conceded a 10-minute period in the third quarter, in which the Bulldogs kicked five-goals-to-none, was symptomatic of a wider issue in his team of not capitalising when the game is on the line. “We won clearances by a lot,” Hardwick said. “We smacked them in contested ball. We smacked them in tackles. We smacked them in inside 50s. “We lost the game.



“At the end of the day, the game looks like a Suns game for 80 per cent (but) for 20 per cent it comes out of reach. “Credit to the Bulldogs, they defended quite well, but we had shots on goal that we should have scored, and we didn’t score. “Our guys are paid to kick goals, and unfortunately, if you don’t, it comes back to haunt you in a close-finishing game.” Arthur Jones shows some dash for the Bulldogs. AFL Photos The Suns’ lack of cutting edge was epitomised by an off day in front of goal for Ben King, with the key forward finishing with 1.4.



Christian Petracca did kick two goals but was also responsible for a crucial third-quarter clanger which allowed Rory Lobb to score during that match-winning burst by the Bulldogs. In a team shorn of Tom Liberatore (soreness) and Riley Garcia (hamstring tightness) and missing Bailey Dale for the first time since 2020, superstar Marcus Bontempelli delivered where the Suns couldn’t - in crucial moments. The Bulldogs’ captain kicked three goals, including two in the first quarter, while Matthew Kennedy celebrated the birth of his second child with three majors of his own. Bailey Humphrey was busy with 29 disposals and 765 metres gained while for the Suns, Petracca and Leo Lombard kicked two goals each with Touk Miller (39 disposals, five tackles, nine clearances) and Matt Rowell (26 disposals, 11 tackles and eight clearances) dominant in midfield. “To come in at halftime and settle, and then have a third quarter like we did was impressive by the boys,” Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge said.



“It probably got a little bit shaky right at the end, but really pleased with the outcome ... we’ve won a few important ones interstate, and this is just as important as any.” Gold Coast travel to face Carlton next week while the Bulldogs are at home against Richmond. AAP Watson and Lewis pile on goals as Hawthorn destroy lowly Tigers



Hawthorn have returned to third on the AFL ladder with a major percentage boost thanks to a brutal 70-point demolition of lowly Richmond at the MCG. The Hawks went into the clash sitting sixth after other results this weekend, but their 18.14 (122) to 6.16 (52) thrashing of the Tigers made a major statement and lifted them back into the top four. Sunday’s final margin flattered Richmond after they kicked several late consolation goals once Hawthorn eased off in the final term. They had led by as much as 87 points during the third quarter. Pointing the way to a win: Hawthorn’s Nick Watson. AFL Photos



Uncontracted Hawk Mitch Lewis dominated up forward with five goals, all in the first half. Goalsneak Nick Watson matched him by also kicking five goals in a stunning first-half performance. The only injury concern for the Hawks was Jack Ginnivan, who was pulled at half-time with the club citing “back soreness.” For Richmond, it was a sour way to commemorate triple premiership player Dion Prestia’s 250th game. The only positive was veteran Tom Lynch finally kicking his 500th goal late in the final term after several weeks stuck on 499.



Tiger Taj Hotton failed to finish the game after suffering an ankle injury, while fellow youngster Steely Green finished the match under a HIA. Jarman Impey is fleet of foot and kicks a running goal on Sunday. AFL Photos Watson, who was back from a two-week injury lay-off, picked up where he left off by kicking the first goal mid-way through the first term after a pedestrian start by both teams. He was able to slot a second goal in the opening quarter but was upstaged by a rampaging Lewis, who kicked three in the first 30 minutes. Lewis would have had four goals by quarter-time had his set shot after the siren not narrowly missed.



But Lewis didn’t have to wait too long for his fourth – which came early in the second term – on his way to five majors. The hapless Tigers went goalless in the first term, and were cruelly denied what would have been a brilliant Seth Campbell goal late in the term by an ARC overrule. Richmond supporters had to wait until the ninth minute of the second quarter to cheer their side’s first major, which came courtesy of Patrick Retschko. View post on X The Tigers had two in a minute after Mykelti Lefau kicked truly, but any joy was short-lived as Hawthorn piled on the next six.



Hawthorn led by a whopping 63 points at the main break, their largest halftime lead in five seasons under coach Sam Mitchell. The Hawks threatened to blow the margin beyond 100 points in the third term before the Tigers were able to make the scoreline more respectable by the final siren. AAP McKay could play through injury for Carlton



Scott Spits, Danny Russell Carlton forward Harry McKay suffered bone bruising and a minor tear in his meniscus after an awkward clash that commentators described as innocuous-looking against Collingwood at the MCG on Saturday night. Scans on Sunday confirmed the prognosis for McKay, who was forced from the field early in the Blues’ 21-point loss to the Magpies that has effectively ruled Carlton out of the wildcard race. McKay bumped knees with teammate Sam Walsh early in the first quarter. Despite the benign nature of the impact, McKay was unable to run and took himself from the ground. Harry McKay suffered bone bruising and a meniscus tear. AFL Photos via Getty Images



His absence left the Carlton forward line short on potency. The Blues said midfielder Adam Cerra, who experienced hamstring tightness and was withdrawn in the second quarter, had not suffered a strain. Carlton said McKay and Cerra would be tested and both may play against Gold Coast at Marvel Stadium next Saturday. Carlton’s caretaker coach Josh Fraser would not be drawn on the severity of McKay’s injury. “Those ones can sometimes look worse than what they appear,” Fraser said after the match. “I don’t know. I haven’t received any more information on it.” Fox Footy commentator David King was perplexed by McKay’s injury. “No one is questioning whether he is injured or not,” he said.



“We are just wondering if it is a pain issue or is it a structural issue. When it has such an influence on the group, it changes six or seven roles in the team, and they were right in the game.” Collingwood coach Craig McRae agreed McKay’s absence for most of the night aided an undermanned Magpies back line. World.title: Families feel pressures as school costs rise. Grandparents are helping
World.content:
NationalEducation Families feel pressures as school costs rise. Grandparents are helping Jackson Graham July 20, 2026 — 12:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than half of families with children at private schools, or who are considering enrolling them, say they are under significant cost pressure, according to new research by the sector’s peak body, which finds most are saving for at least three years to afford the fees. The data, released by Independent Schools Australia on Monday, is from a national sample of 629 families of children at independent schools, and 879 families who are weighing up this option, surveyed between March and April this year. Sandra Masel pays for her grandson’s fees at a private school in Melbourne’s inner east. Joe Armao It found 53 per cent of families were under significant financial pressure, and 57 per cent saved for three or more years for the fees, while 10 per cent saved for more than a decade. Three-quarters of participants said they are adjusting household budgets to afford it, including almost half by reducing holiday spending and cutting non-essentials. A smaller portion of 28 per cent were also cutting essentials, and 18 per cent of respondents were reducing their housing costs.



Related Article Education The biggest losers set to miss out on millions due to private school cash cuts “These are real trade-offs that affect how families live, save and plan. The evidence shows how strongly families value their chosen school. It also shows that the financial commitment to education is not unlimited,” the ISA report finds. It comes as new figures also show Victorian grandparents are financially helping one in 10 families with their child’s schooling, including at government schools, for costs including camps and uniforms. Grandparents in public schooling contribute $1234 annually, compared to $1676 in the Catholic sector and $5593 in the private sector, the Resolve Strategic research commissioned by education bonds company Futurity Investment Group found. Separate research from Independent Schools Australia also found earlier this year that one in five families at private schools received help from other family members for fees. In Victoria, an analysis by this masthead found that schools that had put up their fees had increased them by 5 per cent in the private sector, and many Catholic schools increased their fees by even higher percentages.



Xavier College principal Lee MacMaster said that anecdotally, the school is aware that grandparents in the school community assist with fees. “However, we do not keep data on this,” he said. “We are very grateful for the support of grandparents in supporting the ongoing education of their grandsons at the college.” Some grandparents help pay Xavier College’s school fees. Eddie Jim Sandra Masel, 83, pays the fees for her grandson to attend a private school in Melbourne’s inner east. Masel attended a private school; so did her children, who now face higher living costs and different employment situations than she did at their age. “I figured my grandchild should have the same opportunity, and I can afford it, and they can’t. So it’s a no-brainer, really. I wanted to give them the choice,” Masel said. “Whoever has more money, I think should contribute. There’s no point in making your children wait, and they get the money when they don’t need it any more. They always say you should give with a warm hand, not a cold hand.”



Related Article Exclusive

Education Rooftop tennis courts and Olympic pools: private schools’ multimillion-dollar arms race Masel does not pay for any school camps or extra activities, and said it was completely up to her son’s family where they choose to send their child to school. She said there was no doubt that families faced higher costs of living relative to wages than when she and her late husband paid for their children’s fees themselves. “There’s no question about that. After tax dollars, how can a working couple pay $50,000 a year for each child if they have three kids? It doesn’t stack up.” However, Grandparents Australia director Anne McLeish said there was a worrying trend of older people feeling pressure to pay, especially for activities such as camps at government schools. She was concerned that grandparents could put themselves under too much pressure to contribute to private school fees. “I think that they need to think very carefully about the sacrifices they make to their quality of life to prop up funding education,” McLeish said.



“Grandparents are seduced by the idea that the children need the best quality education, and it’s expensive. It’s not necessarily expensive at all. The best quality education can be determined by looking at the school options and matching the school culture to the family culture.” Families paid $410.3 million to Victorian government schools, the most in Australia, as part of voluntary fees, charges and contributions in 2024, according to the most recent data available from the Australian Curriculum and Assessment Reporting Authority. Jan Dods is paying for her granddaughter Calypso to go on a school ski excursion this term. Ruby Alexander. Eighty-two-year-old Jan Dods has a daughter and a son, and seven grandchildren. Her son sent his children to private schools on part-scholarships, while her daughter’s children attend government schools. Dods’ daughter is a single mother, and Dods has contributed to the grandchildren’s education on this side of the family, including occasionally paying for uniforms and higher costs such as educational trips to China, a young leader trip to Costa Rica and Nicaragua and an art trip to New York City.



Related Article Exclusive

Education ‘Not all about chasing ATARs’: VCE subjects show a clear public-private divide She will fund her youngest granddaughter Calypso to go on a school ski camp to Mount Hotham this term. “I determined that I would try to fill the gaps so that these children would have as much opportunity in the way of stimulating educational experiences as possible,” Dods said. She believed it could last longer than physical gifts. “Education is something that you’ve got in your head and everything else can go,” Dods said. “I have no intention of having a lot of money when I die. I want to give it to them now. They might not need it, or I might not need it. I might not have enough, but I’m being pretty frugal.” The Morning Edition newsletter is our guide to the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. Sign up here.

World.title: Five key takeaways from Pauline Hanson’s Spotlight special
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPauline Hanson Five key takeaways from Pauline Hanson’s Spotlight special William Davis Updated July 19, 2026 — 11:44pm ,first published 10:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pauline Hanson said she loved the idea of mass deportations for Australia, and suggested Tommy Robinson would be welcome Down Under if she became prime minister in a friendly meeting with the convicted criminal. During Seven’s hour-long Spotlight special that tracked Hanson during what she described as a “fact-finding mission” to the UK, the One Nation leader claimed the end of the White Australia Policy had led to problems for Australia, and added she didn’t regret anything – including her push for a “monoculture” and warning the country was at risk of being “swamped” by Asians. Pauline Hanson Spotlight episode on Channel 7. Seven “It’s been really good to come over here on this trip and see what’s happening because it’s really making me determined,” Hanson remarked while walking through the London Borough of Tower Hamlets. Its population is nearly 40 per cent Muslim, the highest proportion of anywhere in England. “I was determined beforehand, but more so now because seeing what’s happened here, I’m going to fight it … I’m not going to have it happen in Australia.”



Here are five key takeaways from the program that aired on Sunday night. Hanson wants to see mass deportations in Australia In the program, Hanson expresses support for radical mass deportations pushed by a fringe party to the right of Reform in the UK. She had, according to journalist Liam Bartlett, been supposed to meet with UK Reform leader and Brexit architect Nigel Farage, however the meeting was scuppered following his decision to resign as an MP in the days prior amid an investigation into his acceptance of funds. Hanson did meet with Restore leader Rupert Lowe who is pushing for mass deportations across the UK. Lowe has called for the removal of 1.8 to 2 million of the UK’s nearly 70 million population.



“Oh, I love it,” she said when asked for her view on mass deportations, confirming she’s “very much on the same page” as the British politician. She did not explain how such a plan would be carried out. Former Neighbours star turned right-wing commentator Holly Valance made a brief cameo during the meeting. Robinson would be welcome to visit Australia under One Nation Pauline Hanson Spotlight episode on Channel 7. Seven



Later in the program Hanson met Robinson, a renowned English racist and convicted criminal whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon. Farage has distanced himself from Robinson and called him a “thug”, while Robinson’s appearance on Karl Stefanovic’s podcast led to Nine axing the Today show host’s lucrative contract. The duo smiled at each other warmly during the meeting, with Robinson saying “the path has been paved by people like Pauline Hanson.” He told her he would like to come to Australia, but falsely claims he’d never tried as he thought his convictions would prevent him getting a visa. He had visas rejected on two previous occasions. “Wait until I’m in, you won’t have … ” she says before being cut off, seemingly from adding “a problem.”



Later asked why she would associate with a man considered too extreme for Reform in the UK, she immediately became defensive. “Why wouldn’t I talk to the man?” Hanson said. “I will say and do what I want to, and I will talk to people if I feel … [I should spend time with] to learn from. “That’s the first time I’ve met Tommy Robinson, and I don’t regret meeting with him.” There’s nothing at all Hanson regrets



Pauline Hanson Spotlight episode on Channel 7. Seven The One Nation leader was later asked if there was anything at all she did regret from her 30 years in public life. “Nothing I can think of,” she said. She specifically defended her calls for a monoculture, describing Islam as a “disease” and early claim Australia was at risk of being “swamped by Asians”. “I will apologise if I’m wrong, but I said it for a reason at the time,” Hanson responded.



“I put my head on the chopping block all the time, and I stand up against the establishment and I say what’s really on my mind.” Barnaby Joyce is on message for One Nation Editor's pick Analysis

Pauline Hanson Hanson knew she had questions to answer. She ran for cover One Nation’s prized Coalition defector stayed on message, and brushed off remarks he’d made in 2017 suggesting Australia would go “down the toilet” if Hanson’s party ever formed government. “Things have changed,” Joyce said. “If people don’t agree with my decision to join One Nation, then I imagine they won’t vote for me, and that’ll be the end of the story.



“You know who else is changing their position … voters.” He suggested there were other big names hoping to join One Nation, and said his boss did have the intellectual capacity to be Prime Minister. Hanson later quipped she didn’t have an ambition to lead the country, but would do it if it were a “necessity”. Joyce reiterated that he did not believe in multiculturalism, and said the Bondi terrorist attack had changed his views on Islam. Hanson cites end of White Australia policy



Asked by Robinson to explain the Australian immigration system and why the country had accepted “violent” people from other places, Hanson pointed to the end of the White Australia Policy. “It started in 1973 with Gough Whitlam. So they opened up and got rid of the White Australia policy,” she said. Related Article Updated

Political leadership ‘Do not apologise for being white’: Hanson takes aim at privilege and trans rights “Then they started bringing in the different migrants, and a lot of them couldn’t speak English, but they learned to speak English.” Hanson then said without evidence many immigrants were moving to Australia to rort the welfare system.



This masthead previously published those comments about the White Australia Policy, and she attacked the reporting on social media as “fake news”. “Never ever have I advocated [for reintroducing the White Australia Policy], and I don’t believe in it as well,” she said in a video published to Facebook. “Yes, I’ve been strong on immigration, bringing the right people in the country in a measured way, and people who want to assimilate and be Australians.” Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy.
